voice.text: Where will the nut end up? Starting underneath everything.
Shake a jar of mixed nuts, or a box of cereal, and the biggest pieces often rise to the top. Scientists call it the Brazil nut effect.
You'd expect heavy things to sink. Yet it happens even when the big pieces are heavier.
Here is one reason. Each shake lifts the grains, and small ones tumble into the gaps under it. It can't fit down there, so it's propped up more each shake.
Scientists have found several effects at work. Grains can flow in a loop, up the walls and down the middle. And in some jars, the big ones sink instead.
Measure it: in this simulation, the big disc climbs from the bottom to near the top. It takes about ten seconds of shaking.
Shaking doesn't just mix things. It often sorts them. Unpopped popcorn kernels sink in a bowl for a related reason.
Next: a coffee drop dries into a ring. Why not a blob?
